# Percutaneous Left Atrial Appendage Closure: A Narrative Review of Clinical Evidence, Technical Aspects, and Future Directions

## Introduction
Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a major driver of ischemic stroke. In patients with non-valvular AF, more than 90% of stroke-inducing thrombi originate within the left atrial appendage (LAA) [1]. Standard stroke prophylaxis revolves around long-term oral anticoagulants (OACs), including vitamin K antagonists and direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs). However, long-term pharmacotherapy is frequently constrained by bleeding complications, poor compliance, and absolute contraindications. To address these limitations, percutaneous left atrial appendage closure (LAAO) has emerged as an established non-pharmacological stroke prevention strategy.

## Clinical Evidence and Pivotal Trials
The clinical efficacy of LAAO was first validated in the landmark PROTECT AF [2] and PREVAIL [3] randomized controlled trials, which compared the first-generation Watchman device (Boston Scientific, Marlborough, MA, USA) against warfarin. A pooled 5-year follow-up of these trials confirmed that LAAO achieves comparable rates of ischemic stroke prevention with a significant reduction in major bleeding, hemorrhagic stroke, and cardiovascular mortality compared to warfarin [4]. Real-world registries, such as the prospective US post-approval experience [5] and the European EWOLUTION registry [6], replicated these findings, demonstrating high procedural success and safety profiles in clinical practice.

For patients with absolute contraindications to long-term OACs, the ASAP study demonstrated that LAAO followed by short-term dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) was safe and efficacious [7]. Similarly, real-world cohorts of patients with prior intracranial hemorrhage have shown substantial clinical benefit from LAAO, with low rates of recurrent bleeding and ischemic events [8]. More recently, the PRAGUE-17 trial compared LAAO directly to DOACs in a high-risk population, establishing non-inferiority for a composite clinical endpoint of stroke, major bleeding, and cardiovascular death [9], an outcome that remained consistent at 4-year follow-up [10].

## Device Landscape and Technical Evolution
The LAAO device landscape has evolved rapidly to optimize safety and efficacy. The next-generation Watchman FLX device features a closed-end design and a larger number of fixation anchors to improve stability and facilitate complete closure. The PINNACLE FLX trial demonstrated excellent safety and high rates of complete LAA closure with this design [11], which has been corroborated by large-scale clinical experience in the NCDR LAAO Registry [12].

Concurrently, the Amplatzer Amulet (Abbott, Chicago, IL, USA) device utilizes a different "disc-and-lobe" design, securing the LAA ostium with a proximal disc while anchoring a distal lobe within the appendage body. In the Amplatzer Amulet IDE trial, the Amulet device was shown to be non-inferior to the Watchman device for ischemic stroke prevention and achieved higher rates of acute LAA sealing, though with a slightly higher rate of peri-procedural complications [13]. While surgical closure during concomitant cardiac operations is also effective, as shown in the LAAOS III trial [14], transcatheter closure remains the standard for minimally invasive, standalone LAA exclusion.

## Procedural Imaging and Technique
Percutaneous LAAO requires precise pre-procedural planning and intraprocedural guidance [15]. This imaging is critical due to the highly variable morphology of the LAA (e.g., "chicken wing", "windsock", "broccoli", or "cactus" shapes) [16]. Multidetector computed tomography (MDCT) is widely used for pre-procedural 3D reconstruction and precise device sizing [17]. Historically, transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) has been the cornerstone of intraprocedural guidance [18]. However, intracardiac echocardiography (ICE) has increasingly been adopted as a reliable alternative that avoids general anesthesia and esophageal intubation [19].

## Complications and Clinical Management
Although LAAO is highly effective, it is not without risks. Major peri-procedural complications include pericardial effusion or cardiac tamponade, device embolization, and vascular access complications, although their rates have decreased significantly as operator experience has grown [20].

Long-term complications of interest include device-related thrombus (DRT) and residual peridevice leak (PDL). DRT occurs in approximately 2% to 4% of cases and is associated with an elevated risk of ischemic stroke [21,22]. Furthermore, significant residual PDL (>5 mm) has been linked to a higher risk of late thromboembolism [23]. Post-procedural management typically involves temporary antithrombotic therapy (either short-term OAC or DAPT), followed by aspirin monotherapy after imaging at 45 days confirms adequate closure. Registries such as EWOLUTION at 1-year [24] and 2-year [25] follow-up have demonstrated that tailored antithrombotic regimens can be safely applied based on individual bleeding risk.

## Current Guidelines and Future Horizons
Professional guidelines from the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) [26], American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology/Heart Rhythm Society (AHA/ACC/HRS) [27], and consensus statements from the European Heart Rhythm Association (EHRA) and European Association of Percutaneous Cardiovascular Interventions (EAPCI) [28] currently recommend LAAO as a Class IIb therapy for patients with AF who have a high stroke risk and clear contraindications to long-term oral anticoagulation.

Future directions are focused on expanding LAAO to broader patient cohorts as a first-line alternative to DOACs. Large-scale trials, such as CHAMPION-AF, are actively comparing LAAO with DOACs in patients with low-to-moderate bleeding risk [29]. Additionally, combining LAAO with catheter ablation of AF in a single-stage procedure has emerged as a feasible and attractive option to simultaneously address both rhythm control and stroke risk [30].
